title: Compensation Benchmarking Report: Market Alignment of Pay Bands, Attrition Risk Assessment, and Recommended Salary Band and Equity Adjustments
subtitle: Compensation Benchmarking | Market Alignment, Attrition Risk Analysis, and Salary Band & Equity Recommendations

document_brief.narrative_theme: This benchmarking study uses market survey data to pinpoint pay misalignment driving attrition risk and to justify targeted salary band adjustments and equity corrections.

sections.heading: Market Benchmarking Methodology and Pay-Band Positioning Results
key_facts: The study benchmarks 48 roles using the Mercer Total Remuneration Survey (TRS) 2025 and the Radford Global Technology Survey 2025.
A market reference point is defined as the 50th percentile (P50), and roles are flagged as below-market when compa-ratio is under 0.90.
The analysis uses a snapshot date of 2026-03-31 for employee pay and job mapping.

sections.heading: Attrition Risk Hotspots and Recommended Salary Band and Equity Corrections
key_facts: Roles with voluntary attrition above 18% in the last 12 months are classified as high attrition risk.
Salary band adjustments are recommended to bring flagged roles to at least 0.95 of market P50 within 90 days of approval.
Equity corrections are triggered when statistically adjusted pay gaps exceed 5% for employees performing the same role and level.

structure.heading: Market Benchmarking Methodology and Pay-Band Positioning Results
text_content: **Market Benchmarking Methodology and Pay-Band Positioning Results**

The benchmarking study comprised 48 roles and used two market data sources: Mercer Total Remuneration Survey (TRS) 2025 and the Radford Global Technology Survey 2025 to establish market pay references. Job-to-survey mapping was performed using role profiles, incumbent responsibilities, and market job matches; conservative alignment rules were applied where a perfect match was not available. For clarity and consistency across sources, surveyed pay values were normalized to local currency equivalents and totaled to comparable remuneration metrics. The market reference point for all comparisons was defined as the 50th percentile (P50) of the combined surveys. Analyses were peer-reviewed by HR analytics.

Compa-ratios were calculated as the incumbent’s total remunerated pay divided by the market reference point (P50). Roles with a compa-ratio under 0.90 were flagged as below-market for immediate attention, consistent with the defined tolerance band. Complementary position bands were defined to facilitate interpretation: below-market (<0.90), market-competitive (0.90–1.10), and above-market (>1.10). Percentile positioning and compa-ratio distributions were produced for each pay band, enabling the identification of central tendency and dispersion across job families. Statistical controls included truncation of extreme outliers and verification against survey population sizes. All calculations treated base salary and role-target variable pay consistently across surveys and currencies globally.

Data cleansing steps included validation of incumbents’ job codes, removal of duplicate records, and normalization of pay components to a total cash view where appropriate. Output files present pay-band positioning as compa-ratio histograms, band medians relative to P50, and role-level summaries for each of the 48 benchmarked roles. Results include recommended target ranges for salary band adjustments and an audit trail; detailed figures and role-level tables are provided in the appendix for executive review.
